info.title: Auto Runtime
info.description: Auto Runtime executes playbooks; Studio manages them; your agent is a separate client. A playbook contains one brain (its reusable functions) and workflows. The brain shares its lifecycle. Functions run directly or through workflows; runs belong to the playbook. Before writing a definition, read its format with get_guide, which also holds what these words mean and the recipes for common tasks. Every operation answers a problem document when it does not succeed, and says in its description what it does, when to use it and which operation to use instead.

post.description: Creates a playbook in the org for one business responsibility, such as reviewing campaign briefs or keeping a team's meeting notes, and returns it, active and empty: its functions and workflows come next. Use it when the person wants a new playbook; list_playbooks shows the playbooks that exist, and an id that is taken or retired is refused. `playbook` is the id every tool inside the playbook takes, `name` is what people call it, and `description` says what the playbook is for, in the person's words.

get.description: Lists the models this server can call, so a reasoning function names one that runs. Each id is what a reasoning function gives as its model, written provider/model; an id that ends in * stands for any model of that provider and is not itself a model to run, and an alias, marked alias, says in resolved_to where it is sent when it may. Use it before a reasoning function names its model, or when a run says its model is not offered. `provider` keeps the models of one provider or gateway, and catalog_status is partial when a provider could not be asked.

get.description: Searches the tools of the tool servers this playbook's functions may use, which a function names in its tools as server/tool or server/*, and execute calls. Without `terms` it lists the servers and, while they offer at most 100 tools together, every tool; with `terms`, the tools whose names, arguments or descriptions hold the words, best first. Each server is asked for its tools when this is called, and one that cannot be asked just now says why in place of its tools. `server` keeps one server, `only` the tools that read or those that may write, and introspect describes a tool whole. Without `playbook` it searches the tool servers of the whole org, naming the playbooks each serves. `providers` lists what a person may connect that no server serves yet.

post.description: Runs a function or workflow with an input and records the run. A run that ends within its call answers its result; a run that finishes later answers started with a run_id unless it ends before its first wait, and get_run shows how it ended. post.description: Answers a request a function's run waits on; the run takes the answer within the host's sweep, a second by default, and an interaction function's run succeeds with it. Use it when the person approves, rejects, revises or otherwise answers a request list_interactions shows, wherever it reached them; a new run asks again and answers nothing, and send_run_event gives an event to a waiting workflow instead. `run_id` is the run of the request, and `answer` takes the shape of the request's answer_schema, which list_interactions shows, such as {"decision": "approve"}. `claimed_for` is whom the caller says it answers for, kept as a claim. The same answer again answers as before, another is a conflict, and one that does not match leaves the request open.

get.description: Lists the open requests of the playbook, newest first: what each function asked, of whom, through which tool, or in the inbox, until when and how its delivery stands, with the `run_id` that answer_interaction takes. Each carries its `answer_schema`, the shape answer_interaction checks an answer against, as recorded when it was asked, which get_definition may no longer show; null for a notification. Use it when the person asks what the playbook is waiting on, or to find the request they answer. `to` keeps the requests to one party, `type` to one type of function and `function` to one name, which with `type` names one function; `cursor` is the next_cursor of the page before. Every reader of the playbook sees each party and message, as a run’s input is seen.

The path names the SHA-256 of the body, and a body whose digest is not the path’s is refused, as is one that breaks the grammar, at its first faulty line; nothing is kept then.

post.description: Gives an event to one workflow run that is still going, for a step that listens for it, such as an approval, and returns the event with its id. An event no step takes yet waits in the run. The playbook's own types and sources, and the lineage attributes it gives its own records, are refused.
